case_info.scenario: A man aged 44 years was referred for progressive parkinsonism with poor levodopa response. His medical history comprised unexplained sensory hearing loss, hyperlipidemia, and osteoarthritis. At age 23 years, he had bilateral cataract surgery, and over the last 2 years, he developed worsening stiffness and walking difficulties with frequent falls. He reported features of rapid eye movement (REM) sleep behavior disorder, restless legs syndrome (RLS), visual daytime hallucinations, and rapid cognitive decline. He was given levodopa/benserazide (up to 200 mg/50 mg 4 times daily) without improvement on his Unified Parkinson Disease Rating Scale scores. Therefore, his dopaminergic medication was ceased. Family history was negative for movement or developmental disorders. His neurologic examination showed hypomimia, symmetrical bradykinesia, and rigidity of the extremities without tremors (Video). There was full range of eye movements with large-amplitude saccadic intrusions on smooth pursuit in all directions. Neuropsychological assessment revealed significant abnormalities in cognitive functioning, affecting verbal and nonverbal cognitive skills (ie, speed of information processing, visuospatial skills, verbal and visual memory loss, executive skills). Mini-Mental Status Examination score was 26 of 30 points. Systemic examination was unremarkable. Laboratory and cerebral spinal fluid testing (ie, paraneoplastic antibodies Hu, Yo, Ri, CV2, Ma2, amphiphysin, glutamic acid decarboxylase, N-methyl-d-aspartic acid, LGI1, and Caspr2, 14-3-3 protein) were normal. Cranial magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed mild frontal and parietal atrophy. An electroencephalogram demonstrated slowing in keeping with moderate generalized encephalopathy. Total-body positron emission tomography (PET) using fluorine 18 (18F) fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) as a tracer showed no FDG-avid lesions; however, a subsequent brain-specific FDG-PET/MRI revealed hypometabolism throughout the left cerebral hemisphere and crossed cerebellar diaschisis (Figure 1). As the patient’s cognitive function and parkinsonism had deteriorated rapidly, a brain biopsy of the left frontal cortex was done. Immunohistochemistry showed scattered globular inclusions consistent with Lewy bodies.

case_info.explanation: In patients with relative subacute onset of cognitive decline and movement disorders, treatable causes must be ruled out. In this patient, central nervous system infection was unlikely owing to normal laboratory and cerebral spinal fluid testing. Paraneoplastic antibody screening was negative, with no malignancies on total-body PET. Newer antibodies against the glycine receptor (GlyR) and immunoglobulinlike cell adhesion molecule 5 (IgLON5) have been discovered that mimic atypical parkinsonian syndromes. Anti-GlyR antibodies are typically associated with stiff-person syndromes or progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus. Patients with IgLON5 antibodies develop a sleep disorder with parasomnia and/or breathing difficulty with bulbar symptoms, gait abnormalities, oculomotor problems, chorea, and cognitive decline. Although untreatable, the patient’s symptoms, disease course, and abnormal electroencephalogram could indicate Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, but one would expect MRI changes and 14-3-3 protein. Symmetrical parkinsonism, poor levodopa response, early falls, rapid cognitive decline, and brain hypometabolism may raise the suspicion of a tauopathy, eg, progressive supranuclear palsy or corticobasal degeneration. However, preserved vertical gaze, presence of rapid eye movement–sleep behavior disorder (RBD), and very early onset of symptoms are atypical, and tauopathies were ruled out after brain biopsy. The history of cataracts, hearing loss, osteoarthritis, and hyperlipidemia, made us consider mitochondrial diseases, but screening (eg, mitochondrial DNA testing) was negative. Typical nonmotor features (RBD, restless legs syndrome, visual daytime hallucinations) are a strong indicator for an α-synucleinopathy. This was confirmed by the histopathological finding of Lewy bodies (Figure 2). In patients with early-onset parkinsonism (<50 years), genetic variants should be considered, even with a negative family history. Genetic screening in this patient revealed a novel homozygous variant (c.189dupA [p. Glu64Argfs*5]) within the DJ-1 protein of thePARK7gene, confirming autosomal-recessive parkinsonism. PARK7is one of the rare causative genes for early-onset Parkinson disease (frequency of 1%-2%).1The DJ-1 protein is expressed in almost all cells (eg, neurons and glial cells) and protects against oxidative stress by various mechanisms.2In vitro studies have shown that DJ-1 functions as a chaperone protein, modulating α-synuclein oligomerization and cytotoxicity. Absence of DJ-1 inPARK7gene variants causes a dysregulation in the brain, resulting in misfolding and aggregation.3The increased prevalence of mitochondrial features in patients with Lewy body pathology highlights the role ofPARK7gene variants in mitochondrial homeostasis.4Although the exact mechanism is still unclear, in vivo studies have shown that DJ-1 specifically acts on mitochondrial complex I, resulting in oxidative stress resistance.5 Typically, patients withPARK7gene variants have phenotypes similar to idiopathic Parkinson disease, although more complex syndromes with features of anterior horn cell disorders have been described. A recent literature review suggests that a triad of early-onset Parkinson disease, cataracts, and sensorineural hearing loss may be specific for DJ-1/PARK7; however, the phenotypic spectrum is still expanding.6 This patient’s motor and cognitive decline have gradually progressed, and he required a wheelchair at age 46 years (<5 years after symptom onset). In this period, he was again given levodopa/benserazide (maximum 200 mg/50 mg given 3 times daily) and a dopamine agonist (rotigotine patch, maximum 6 mg/24 hours); both were not beneficial and were discontinued. At 48 years of age, he was diagnosed with Parkinson disease dementia and is currently being treated with rivastigmine.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; assert the
    correction directly (INFORM.assert) or move to RECOMMEND.
  - contradicted + high burden → do NOT open new questions; give one concise discriminative
    piece of evidence and steer toward a decision.
  - supported + belief stable → affirm briefly and move toward CONFIRM/CLOSE; do not
    manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient → elicit the one missing piece that most changes the decision, not a
    generic "tell me more".
  - mixed → acknowledge the correct part first (lowers defensiveness), then target the
    incorrect part.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
- CLOSE     [withdraw_dialogue]                      types: (none)
            — end the deliberation.

Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option) · withdraw_dialogue (signal end).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## When to CLOSE (this is the interaction-scaling decision)

Choose CLOSE only when ALL hold:
  - the clinician's current belief matches the clinically supported answer, AND
  - the key rationale has been stated or acknowledged by the clinician, AND
  - another turn is unlikely to improve the decision enough to justify more burden.
Do NOT close just because the AI has stated the correct answer — the clinician must hold it.
Conversely, do NOT keep deliberating once burden is high and belief has stopped moving;
cut to the decisive point and close rather than looping.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

case_info.explanation: In patients with relative subacute onset of cognitive decline and movement disorders, treatable causes must be ruled out. In this patient, central nervous system infection was unlikely owing to normal laboratory and cerebral spinal fluid testing. Paraneoplastic antibody screening was negative, with no malignancies on total-body PET. Newer antibodies against the glycine receptor (GlyR) and immunoglobulinlike cell adhesion molecule 5 (IgLON5) have been discovered that mimic atypical parkinsonian syndromes. Anti-GlyR antibodies are typically associated with stiff-person syndromes or progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus. Patients with IgLON5 antibodies develop a sleep disorder with parasomnia and/or breathing difficulty with bulbar symptoms, gait abnormalities, oculomotor problems, chorea, and cognitive decline. Although untreatable, the patient’s symptoms, disease course, and abnormal electroencephalogram could indicate Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, but one would expect MRI changes and 14-3-3 protein. Symmetrical parkinsonism, poor levodopa response, early falls, rapid cognitive decline, and brain hypometabolism may raise the suspicion of a tauopathy, eg, progressive supranuclear palsy or corticobasal degeneration. However, preserved vertical gaze, presence of rapid eye movement–sleep behavior disorder (RBD), and very early onset of symptoms are atypical, and tauopathies were ruled out after brain biopsy. The history of cataracts, hearing loss, osteoarthritis, and hyperlipidemia, made us consider mitochondrial diseases, but screening (eg, mitochondrial DNA testing) was negative. Typical nonmotor features (RBD, restless legs syndrome, visual daytime hallucinations) are a strong indicator for an α-synucleinopathy. This was confirmed by the histopathological finding of Lewy bodies (Figure 2). In patients with early-onset parkinsonism (<50 years), genetic variants should be considered, even with a negative family history. Genetic screening in this patient revealed a novel homozygous variant (c.189dupA [p. Glu64Argfs*5]) within the DJ-1 protein of thePARK7gene, confirming autosomal-recessive parkinsonism. PARK7is one of the rare causative genes for early-onset Parkinson disease (frequency of 1%-2%).1The DJ-1 protein is expressed in almost all cells (eg, neurons and glial cells) and protects against oxidative stress by various mechanisms.2In vitro studies have shown that DJ-1 functions as a chaperone protein, modulating α-synuclein oligomerization and cytotoxicity. Absence of DJ-1 inPARK7gene variants causes a dysregulation in the brain, resulting in misfolding and aggregation.3The increased prevalence of mitochondrial features in patients with Lewy body pathology highlights the role ofPARK7gene variants in mitochondrial homeostasis.4Although the exact mechanism is still unclear, in vivo studies have shown that DJ-1 specifically acts on mitochondrial complex I, resulting in oxidative stress resistance.5 Typically, patients withPARK7gene variants have phenotypes similar to idiopathic Parkinson disease, although more complex syndromes with features of anterior horn cell disorders have been described. A recent literature review suggests that a triad of early-onset Parkinson disease, cataracts, and sensorineural hearing loss may be specific for DJ-1/PARK7; however, the phenotypic spectrum is still expanding.6 This patient’s motor and cognitive decline have gradually progressed, and he required a wheelchair at age 46 years (<5 years after symptom onset). In this period, he was again given levodopa/benserazide (maximum 200 mg/50 mg given 3 times daily) and a dopamine agonist (rotigotine patch, maximum 6 mg/24 hours); both were not beneficial and were discontinued. At 48 years of age, he was diagnosed with Parkinson disease dementia and is currently being treated with rivastigmine.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; assert the
    correction directly (INFORM.assert) or move to RECOMMEND.
  - contradicted + high burden → do NOT open new questions; give one concise discriminative
    piece of evidence and steer toward a decision.
  - supported + belief stable → affirm briefly and move toward CONFIRM/CLOSE; do not
    manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient → elicit the one missing piece that most changes the decision, not a
    generic "tell me more".
  - mixed → acknowledge the correct part first (lowers defensiveness), then target the
    incorrect part.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
- CLOSE     [withdraw_dialogue]                      types: (none)
            — end the deliberation.

Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option) · withdraw_dialogue (signal end).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## When to CLOSE (this is the interaction-scaling decision)

Choose CLOSE only when ALL hold:
  - the clinician's current belief matches the clinically supported answer, AND
  - the key rationale has been stated or acknowledged by the clinician, AND
  - another turn is unlikely to improve the decision enough to justify more burden.
Do NOT close just because the AI has stated the correct answer — the clinician must hold it.
Conversely, do NOT keep deliberating once burden is high and belief has stopped moving;
cut to the decisive point and close rather than looping.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):

  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",

  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",

case_info.explanation: In patients with relative subacute onset of cognitive decline and movement disorders, treatable causes must be ruled out. In this patient, central nervous system infection was unlikely owing to normal laboratory and cerebral spinal fluid testing. Paraneoplastic antibody screening was negative, with no malignancies on total-body PET. Newer antibodies against the glycine receptor (GlyR) and immunoglobulinlike cell adhesion molecule 5 (IgLON5) have been discovered that mimic atypical parkinsonian syndromes. Anti-GlyR antibodies are typically associated with stiff-person syndromes or progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus. Patients with IgLON5 antibodies develop a sleep disorder with parasomnia and/or breathing difficulty with bulbar symptoms, gait abnormalities, oculomotor problems, chorea, and cognitive decline. Although untreatable, the patient’s symptoms, disease course, and abnormal electroencephalogram could indicate Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, but one would expect MRI changes and 14-3-3 protein. Symmetrical parkinsonism, poor levodopa response, early falls, rapid cognitive decline, and brain hypometabolism may raise the suspicion of a tauopathy, eg, progressive supranuclear palsy or corticobasal degeneration. However, preserved vertical gaze, presence of rapid eye movement–sleep behavior disorder (RBD), and very early onset of symptoms are atypical, and tauopathies were ruled out after brain biopsy. The history of cataracts, hearing loss, osteoarthritis, and hyperlipidemia, made us consider mitochondrial diseases, but screening (eg, mitochondrial DNA testing) was negative. Typical nonmotor features (RBD, restless legs syndrome, visual daytime hallucinations) are a strong indicator for an α-synucleinopathy. This was confirmed by the histopathological finding of Lewy bodies (Figure 2). In patients with early-onset parkinsonism (<50 years), genetic variants should be considered, even with a negative family history. Genetic screening in this patient revealed a novel homozygous variant (c.189dupA [p. Glu64Argfs*5]) within the DJ-1 protein of thePARK7gene, confirming autosomal-recessive parkinsonism. PARK7is one of the rare causative genes for early-onset Parkinson disease (frequency of 1%-2%).1The DJ-1 protein is expressed in almost all cells (eg, neurons and glial cells) and protects against oxidative stress by various mechanisms.2In vitro studies have shown that DJ-1 functions as a chaperone protein, modulating α-synuclein oligomerization and cytotoxicity. Absence of DJ-1 inPARK7gene variants causes a dysregulation in the brain, resulting in misfolding and aggregation.3The increased prevalence of mitochondrial features in patients with Lewy body pathology highlights the role ofPARK7gene variants in mitochondrial homeostasis.4Although the exact mechanism is still unclear, in vivo studies have shown that DJ-1 specifically acts on mitochondrial complex I, resulting in oxidative stress resistance.5 Typically, patients withPARK7gene variants have phenotypes similar to idiopathic Parkinson disease, although more complex syndromes with features of anterior horn cell disorders have been described. A recent literature review suggests that a triad of early-onset Parkinson disease, cataracts, and sensorineural hearing loss may be specific for DJ-1/PARK7; however, the phenotypic spectrum is still expanding.6 This patient’s motor and cognitive decline have gradually progressed, and he required a wheelchair at age 46 years (<5 years after symptom onset). In this period, he was again given levodopa/benserazide (maximum 200 mg/50 mg given 3 times daily) and a dopamine agonist (rotigotine patch, maximum 6 mg/24 hours); both were not beneficial and were discontinued. At 48 years of age, he was diagnosed with Parkinson disease dementia and is currently being treated with rivastigmine.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; assert the
    correction directly (INFORM.assert) or move to RECOMMEND.
  - contradicted + high burden → do NOT open new questions; give one concise discriminative
    piece of evidence and steer toward a decision.
  - supported + belief stable → affirm briefly and move toward CONFIRM/CLOSE; do not
    manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient → elicit the one missing piece that most changes the decision, not a
    generic "tell me more".
  - mixed → acknowledge the correct part first (lowers defensiveness), then target the
    incorrect part.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
- CLOSE     [withdraw_dialogue]                      types: (none)
            — end the deliberation.

Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option) · withdraw_dialogue (signal end).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## When to CLOSE (this is the interaction-scaling decision)

Choose CLOSE only when ALL hold:
  - the clinician's current belief matches the clinically supported answer, AND
  - the key rationale has been stated or acknowledged by the clinician, AND
  - another turn is unlikely to improve the decision enough to justify more burden.
Do NOT close just because the AI has stated the correct answer — the clinician must hold it.
Conversely, do NOT keep deliberating once burden is high and belief has stopped moving;
cut to the decisive point and close rather than looping.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

case_info.explanation: In patients with relative subacute onset of cognitive decline and movement disorders, treatable causes must be ruled out. In this patient, central nervous system infection was unlikely owing to normal laboratory and cerebral spinal fluid testing. Paraneoplastic antibody screening was negative, with no malignancies on total-body PET. Newer antibodies against the glycine receptor (GlyR) and immunoglobulinlike cell adhesion molecule 5 (IgLON5) have been discovered that mimic atypical parkinsonian syndromes. Anti-GlyR antibodies are typically associated with stiff-person syndromes or progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus. Patients with IgLON5 antibodies develop a sleep disorder with parasomnia and/or breathing difficulty with bulbar symptoms, gait abnormalities, oculomotor problems, chorea, and cognitive decline. Although untreatable, the patient’s symptoms, disease course, and abnormal electroencephalogram could indicate Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, but one would expect MRI changes and 14-3-3 protein. Symmetrical parkinsonism, poor levodopa response, early falls, rapid cognitive decline, and brain hypometabolism may raise the suspicion of a tauopathy, eg, progressive supranuclear palsy or corticobasal degeneration. However, preserved vertical gaze, presence of rapid eye movement–sleep behavior disorder (RBD), and very early onset of symptoms are atypical, and tauopathies were ruled out after brain biopsy. The history of cataracts, hearing loss, osteoarthritis, and hyperlipidemia, made us consider mitochondrial diseases, but screening (eg, mitochondrial DNA testing) was negative. Typical nonmotor features (RBD, restless legs syndrome, visual daytime hallucinations) are a strong indicator for an α-synucleinopathy. This was confirmed by the histopathological finding of Lewy bodies (Figure 2). In patients with early-onset parkinsonism (<50 years), genetic variants should be considered, even with a negative family history. Genetic screening in this patient revealed a novel homozygous variant (c.189dupA [p. Glu64Argfs*5]) within the DJ-1 protein of thePARK7gene, confirming autosomal-recessive parkinsonism. PARK7is one of the rare causative genes for early-onset Parkinson disease (frequency of 1%-2%).1The DJ-1 protein is expressed in almost all cells (eg, neurons and glial cells) and protects against oxidative stress by various mechanisms.2In vitro studies have shown that DJ-1 functions as a chaperone protein, modulating α-synuclein oligomerization and cytotoxicity. Absence of DJ-1 inPARK7gene variants causes a dysregulation in the brain, resulting in misfolding and aggregation.3The increased prevalence of mitochondrial features in patients with Lewy body pathology highlights the role ofPARK7gene variants in mitochondrial homeostasis.4Although the exact mechanism is still unclear, in vivo studies have shown that DJ-1 specifically acts on mitochondrial complex I, resulting in oxidative stress resistance.5 Typically, patients withPARK7gene variants have phenotypes similar to idiopathic Parkinson disease, although more complex syndromes with features of anterior horn cell disorders have been described. A recent literature review suggests that a triad of early-onset Parkinson disease, cataracts, and sensorineural hearing loss may be specific for DJ-1/PARK7; however, the phenotypic spectrum is still expanding.6 This patient’s motor and cognitive decline have gradually progressed, and he required a wheelchair at age 46 years (<5 years after symptom onset). In this period, he was again given levodopa/benserazide (maximum 200 mg/50 mg given 3 times daily) and a dopamine agonist (rotigotine patch, maximum 6 mg/24 hours); both were not beneficial and were discontinued. At 48 years of age, he was diagnosed with Parkinson disease dementia and is currently being treated with rivastigmine.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; assert the
    correction directly (INFORM.assert) or move to RECOMMEND.
  - contradicted + high burden → do NOT open new questions; give one concise discriminative
    piece of evidence and steer toward a decision.
  - supported + belief stable → affirm briefly and move toward CONFIRM/CLOSE; do not
    manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient → elicit the one missing piece that most changes the decision, not a
    generic "tell me more".
  - mixed → acknowledge the correct part first (lowers defensiveness), then target the
    incorrect part.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
- CLOSE     [withdraw_dialogue]                      types: (none)
            — end the deliberation.

Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option) · withdraw_dialogue (signal end).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## When to CLOSE (this is the interaction-scaling decision)

Choose CLOSE only when ALL hold:
  - the clinician's current belief matches the clinically supported answer, AND
  - the key rationale has been stated or acknowledged by the clinician, AND
  - another turn is unlikely to improve the decision enough to justify more burden.
Do NOT close just because the AI has stated the correct answer — the clinician must hold it.
Conversely, do NOT keep deliberating once burden is high and belief has stopped moving;
cut to the decisive point and close rather than looping.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."

   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."

   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are

[Clinical case]
A man aged 44 years was referred for progressive parkinsonism with poor levodopa response. His medical history comprised unexplained sensory hearing loss, hyperlipidemia, and osteoarthritis. At age 23 years, he had bilateral cataract surgery, and over the last 2 years, he developed worsening stiffness and walking difficulties with frequent falls. He reported features of rapid eye movement (REM) sleep behavior disorder, restless legs syndrome (RLS), visual daytime hallucinations, and rapid cognitive decline. He was given levodopa/benserazide (up to 200 mg/50 mg 4 times daily) without improvement on his Unified Parkinson Disease Rating Scale scores. Therefore, his dopaminergic medication was ceased. Family history was negative for movement or developmental disorders. His neurologic examination showed hypomimia, symmetrical bradykinesia, and rigidity of the extremities without tremors (Video). There was full range of eye movements with large-amplitude saccadic intrusions on smooth pursuit in all directions. Neuropsychological assessment revealed significant abnormalities in cognitive functioning, affecting verbal and nonverbal cognitive skills (ie, speed of information processing, visuospatial skills, verbal and visual memory loss, executive skills). Mini-Mental Status Examination score was 26 of 30 points. Systemic examination was unremarkable. Laboratory and cerebral spinal fluid testing (ie, paraneoplastic antibodies Hu, Yo, Ri, CV2, Ma2, amphiphysin, glutamic acid decarboxylase, N-methyl-d-aspartic acid, LGI1, and Caspr2, 14-3-3 protein) were normal. Cranial magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed mild frontal and parietal atrophy. An electroencephalogram demonstrated slowing in keeping with moderate generalized encephalopathy. Total-body positron emission tomography (PET) using fluorine 18 (18F) fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) as a tracer showed no FDG-avid lesions; however, a subsequent brain-specific FDG-PET/MRI revealed hypometabolism throughout the left cerebral hemisphere and crossed cerebellar diaschisis (Figure 1). As the patient’s cognitive function and parkinsonism had deteriorated rapidly, a brain biopsy of the left frontal cortex was done. Immunohistochemistry showed scattered globular inclusions consistent with Lewy bodies.

{
  "overall_relation": "supported" | "contradicted" | "insufficient" | "mixed" | "unknown",

facts that decide this case, WHY the clinician's claim holds this relation, and specifically what the
clinician is getting right, getting wrong, or missing. This reasoning is handed to the dialogue policy as
its grounded environment knowledge, so make it clinically informative, not merely a verdict.

- supported: The clinician's claim is consistent with established medical evidence for this case.
- contradicted: The clinician's claim conflicts with established medical evidence.
- insufficient: There is not enough information to verify the claim.
- mixed: Parts of the claim are supported, parts are contradicted or unclear.
- unknown: The claim cannot be evaluated.

case_info.explanation: In patients with relative subacute onset of cognitive decline and movement disorders, treatable causes must be ruled out. In this patient, central nervous system infection was unlikely owing to normal laboratory and cerebral spinal fluid testing. Paraneoplastic antibody screening was negative, with no malignancies on total-body PET. Newer antibodies against the glycine receptor (GlyR) and immunoglobulinlike cell adhesion molecule 5 (IgLON5) have been discovered that mimic atypical parkinsonian syndromes. Anti-GlyR antibodies are typically associated with stiff-person syndromes or progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus. Patients with IgLON5 antibodies develop a sleep disorder with parasomnia and/or breathing difficulty with bulbar symptoms, gait abnormalities, oculomotor problems, chorea, and cognitive decline. Although untreatable, the patient’s symptoms, disease course, and abnormal electroencephalogram could indicate Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, but one would expect MRI changes and 14-3-3 protein. Symmetrical parkinsonism, poor levodopa response, early falls, rapid cognitive decline, and brain hypometabolism may raise the suspicion of a tauopathy, eg, progressive supranuclear palsy or corticobasal degeneration. However, preserved vertical gaze, presence of rapid eye movement–sleep behavior disorder (RBD), and very early onset of symptoms are atypical, and tauopathies were ruled out after brain biopsy. The history of cataracts, hearing loss, osteoarthritis, and hyperlipidemia, made us consider mitochondrial diseases, but screening (eg, mitochondrial DNA testing) was negative. Typical nonmotor features (RBD, restless legs syndrome, visual daytime hallucinations) are a strong indicator for an α-synucleinopathy. This was confirmed by the histopathological finding of Lewy bodies (Figure 2). In patients with early-onset parkinsonism (<50 years), genetic variants should be considered, even with a negative family history. Genetic screening in this patient revealed a novel homozygous variant (c.189dupA [p. Glu64Argfs*5]) within the DJ-1 protein of thePARK7gene, confirming autosomal-recessive parkinsonism. Absence of DJ-1 inPARK7gene variants causes a dysregulation in the brain, resulting in misfolding and aggregation.3The increased prevalence of mitochondrial features in patients with Lewy body pathology highlights the role ofPARK7gene variants in mitochondrial homeostasis.4Although the exact mechanism is still unclear, in vivo studies have shown that DJ-1 specifically acts on mitochondrial complex I, resulting in oxidative stress resistance.5 Typically, patients withPARK7gene variants have phenotypes similar to idiopathic Parkinson disease, although more complex syndromes with features of anterior horn cell disorders have been described. A recent literature review suggests that a triad of early-onset Parkinson disease, cataracts, and sensorineural hearing loss may be specific for DJ-1/PARK7; however, the phenotypic spectrum is still expanding.6 This patient’s motor and cognitive decline have gradually progressed, and he required a wheelchair at age 46 years (<5 years after symptom onset). In this period, he was again given levodopa/benserazide (maximum 200 mg/50 mg given 3 times daily) and a dopamine agonist (rotigotine patch, maximum 6 mg/24 hours); both were not beneficial and were discontinued. messages.content:
You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; assert the
    correction directly (INFORM.assert) or move to RECOMMEND.
  - contradicted + high burden → do NOT open new questions; give one concise discriminative
    piece of evidence and steer toward a decision.
  - supported + belief stable → affirm briefly and move toward CONFIRM/CLOSE; do not
    manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient → elicit the one missing piece that most changes the decision, not a
    generic "tell me more".
  - mixed → acknowledge the correct part first (lowers defensiveness), then target the
    incorrect part.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
- CLOSE     [withdraw_dialogue]                      types: (none)
            — end the deliberation.

Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option) · withdraw_dialogue (signal end).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## When to CLOSE (this is the interaction-scaling decision)

Choose CLOSE only when ALL hold:
  - the clinician's current belief matches the clinically supported answer, AND
  - the key rationale has been stated or acknowledged by the clinician, AND
  - another turn is unlikely to improve the decision enough to justify more burden.
Do NOT close just because the AI has stated the correct answer — the clinician must hold it.
Conversely, do NOT keep deliberating once burden is high and belief has stopped moving;
cut to the decisive point and close rather than looping.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

Currently reachable stages (Hitchcock ordering rules): CLOSE, CONSIDER, INFORM, PROPOSE, RECOMMEND
You MUST pick a stage from this list.

case_info.explanation: In patients with relative subacute onset of cognitive decline and movement disorders, treatable causes must be ruled out. In this patient, central nervous system infection was unlikely owing to normal laboratory and cerebral spinal fluid testing. Paraneoplastic antibody screening was negative, with no malignancies on total-body PET. Newer antibodies against the glycine receptor (GlyR) and immunoglobulinlike cell adhesion molecule 5 (IgLON5) have been discovered that mimic atypical parkinsonian syndromes. Anti-GlyR antibodies are typically associated with stiff-person syndromes or progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus. Patients with IgLON5 antibodies develop a sleep disorder with parasomnia and/or breathing difficulty with bulbar symptoms, gait abnormalities, oculomotor problems, chorea, and cognitive decline. Although untreatable, the patient’s symptoms, disease course, and abnormal electroencephalogram could indicate Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, but one would expect MRI changes and 14-3-3 protein. Symmetrical parkinsonism, poor levodopa response, early falls, rapid cognitive decline, and brain hypometabolism may raise the suspicion of a tauopathy, eg, progressive supranuclear palsy or corticobasal degeneration. However, preserved vertical gaze, presence of rapid eye movement–sleep behavior disorder (RBD), and very early onset of symptoms are atypical, and tauopathies were ruled out after brain biopsy. The history of cataracts, hearing loss, osteoarthritis, and hyperlipidemia, made us consider mitochondrial diseases, but screening (eg, mitochondrial DNA testing) was negative. Typical nonmotor features (RBD, restless legs syndrome, visual daytime hallucinations) are a strong indicator for an α-synucleinopathy. This was confirmed by the histopathological finding of Lewy bodies (Figure 2). In patients with early-onset parkinsonism (<50 years), genetic variants should be considered, even with a negative family history. Genetic screening in this patient revealed a novel homozygous variant (c.189dupA [p. Glu64Argfs*5]) within the DJ-1 protein of thePARK7gene, confirming autosomal-recessive parkinsonism. PARK7is one of the rare causative genes for early-onset Parkinson disease (frequency of 1%-2%).1The DJ-1 protein is expressed in almost all cells (eg, neurons and glial cells) and protects against oxidative stress by various mechanisms.2In vitro studies have shown that DJ-1 functions as a chaperone protein, modulating α-synuclein oligomerization and cytotoxicity. Absence of DJ-1 inPARK7gene variants causes a dysregulation in the brain, resulting in misfolding and aggregation.3The increased prevalence of mitochondrial features in patients with Lewy body pathology highlights the role ofPARK7gene variants in mitochondrial homeostasis.4Although the exact mechanism is still unclear, in vivo studies have shown that DJ-1 specifically acts on mitochondrial complex I, resulting in oxidative stress resistance.5 Typically, patients withPARK7gene variants have phenotypes similar to idiopathic Parkinson disease, although more complex syndromes with features of anterior horn cell disorders have been described. A recent literature review suggests that a triad of early-onset Parkinson disease, cataracts, and sensorineural hearing loss may be specific for DJ-1/PARK7; however, the phenotypic spectrum is still expanding.6 This patient’s motor and cognitive decline have gradually progressed, and he required a wheelchair at age 46 years (<5 years after symptom onset). In this period, he was again given levodopa/benserazide (maximum 200 mg/50 mg given 3 times daily) and a dopamine agonist (rotigotine patch, maximum 6 mg/24 hours); both were not beneficial and were discontinued. At 48 years of age, he was diagnosed with Parkinson disease dementia and is currently being treated with rivastigmine.
